compiler_and_flags: icc, clang and gcc mentioned; flags not stated (JIT generated kernels)
hardware: Intel Xeon 8480+ (SPR), AWS Graviton 3, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel i9-12900K
stars_or_usage: 977 stars; used by PyTorch/IPEX, CP2K, SeisSol
tradeoffs: JIT code generation; C API (also C++ headers); PARLOOPER loop layer lives in other repos (tpp-pytorch-extension).
caveats: Numbers are from the PARLOOPER paper, whose artifact/benchmark code link was not confirmed on the page; evidence is arXiv preprint (peer-review status not confirmed) so capped at C. Repo root page has no benchmark numbers.
name: LIBXSMM / PARLOOPER (TPP kernels)
workload: BF16 GEMM, ResNet-50 convolutions, BERT-Large training and block-sparse BERT inference using Tensor Processing Primitives with JIT code generation on SPR, Graviton 3, Zen4 and Alder Lake CPUs.
claimed_speedup: GEMM up to 1.98x over oneDNN on SPR BF16, up to 1.45x on Graviton 3; ResNet-50 conv geomean 1.16x (SPR), 1.75x (GVT3), 1.12x (Zen4), 1.14x (ADL); BERT-Large training 3.3x over IPEX with oneDNN
found_via: arXiv web search: 'arXiv deep learning operator kernel library faster than oneDNN XNNPACK ...' then arxiv.org/html/2304.12576v2

compiler_and_flags: NVCC, CUDA 12.3, cuDNN 9.1.1.17, CUTLASS 3.5; GPU clock fixed at 1830 MHz
tradeoffs: Hopper-only for FA3 path; Python/PyTorch front end with CUDA C++ kernels (CUTLASS-based); GPU-only.
caveats: NeurIPS 2024 paper; benchmark script location in repo not opened, so tier B not A. Not uniformly faster than cuDNN (FP8 causal). cuDNN has since added its own FA-style kernels, so the gap may have narrowed.
name: FlashAttention-3 (flash-attention)
workload: FP16/BF16 and FP8 attention forward pass on H100 SXM5 across sequence lengths and head dims.
claimed_speedup: FP16 forward up to 740 TFLOPs/s (75% utilization); outperforms cuDNN for sequence length >= 1k, up to 1.5x faster in some configs; FP8 mixed (lags cuDNN for hdim128/256 causal)
found_via: WebSearch: ThunderKittens CUDA C++ kernels attention faster than cuDNN FlashAttention-3

stars_or_usage: 3.7k stars; used by Together AI, Jump Trading, Cursor (per README)
tradeoffs: NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell only (Ampere no longer supported); needs CUDA 12.8+; AMD via separate HipKittens.
caveats: First-party arXiv preprint; compiler flags and full benchmark code not verified. Matches rather than beats cuBLAS/FA3 on forward; wins are on backward and non-standard baselines. cuDNN not the headline baseline.
name: ThunderKittens
baseline: cuBLAS GEMM and FlashAttention-3 / cuDNN attention
workload: Header-only C++20/CUDA tile primitives for GEMM, attention forward/backward, linear attention and SSM kernels on H100.
claimed_speedup: matches cuBLAS and FlashAttention-3 on GEMM and attention forward; 10-40% faster on attention backward; 14x faster than Flash Linear Attention; 8x faster than FlashFFTConv; README: 855 TFLOPs on H100 GEMM (86% of peak)
found_via: WebSearch: ThunderKittens ... faster than cuDNN FlashAttention-3

hardware: Apple M2 Ultra; Intel Core i7-13700H
tradeoffs: Requires ternary-trained models; built on llama.cpp infrastructure.
caveats: Baseline is FP16 llama.cpp on a different (larger) weight format, so the speedup partly reflects 1.58-bit weights, not a like-for-like kernel win; compiler flags not stated; not one of the listed baselines.
name: BitNet (bitnet.cpp)
workload: Ternary (1.58-bit) LLM CPU inference with I2_S, TL1, TL2 kernels versus llama.cpp FP16.
claimed_speedup: x86 2.37x to 6.17x (up to 6.46x with 2 threads) with 71.9-82.2% energy reduction; ARM 1.37x to 5.07x with 55.4-70.0% energy savings
found_via: WebSearch: quantized LLM inference CPU kernels C++ faster than llama.cpp

hardware: 4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable, single socket
caveats: Repo archived 2024-08-30, Intel ceased maintenance. The paper links intel-extension-for-transformers (archived 2024-10-25, 2.2k stars, Apache-2.0) as code location. Compiler flags not stated. Baseline llama.cpp is not a listed incumbent.
name: Intel Neural Speed / LLM Runtime
workload: INT4 LLM inference next-token latency on 4th Gen Xeon (GPT-J 6B, Llama-2 7B, GPT-NeoX 20B) with AVX2/AVX512/VNNI/AMX kernels.
claimed_speedup: up to 1.6x faster than ggml-based at group size 128 and 1.3x at group size 32 (e.g. GPT-J 6B 19.98 ms vs 31.62 ms); README claims up to 40x vs llama.cpp (Medium link, not verified)
found_via: WebSearch: quantized LLM inference CPU kernels ...; arxiv.org/abs/2311.00502

compiler_and_flags: direct x86 assembly generation, no compiler flags
hardware: AWS AMD Epyc 7R32 (AVX2); Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX512)
tradeoffs: Needs sparse (pruned) weights; Python API has ctypes overhead; C++ API used in paper benchmarks.
caveats: Sparse convolution generator and inference engine were not open-sourced. oneDNN/XNNPACK not directly compared; baselines are LIBXSMM, MKL, OpenVINO. Paper-only benchmark, 22% slower on AMD vs SkimCaffe.
name: SparseDNN
workload: Sparse matrix kernels generated as x86 assembly with autotuning; end-to-end pruneBERT inference.
claimed_speedup: 2.5x geomean over LIBXSMM single-threaded on Intel (1.3x on AMD); 4x over dense BLAS at 95% sparsity (break-even ~70%); up to 5x throughput vs OpenVINO on pruneBERT
found_via: WebSearch: arXiv deep learning operator kernel library faster than oneDNN XNNPACK ...

tradeoffs: Embedded as a component of oneDNN; fusion gains only for graph-level patterns.
caveats: Paper only for this entry: the paper points to the oneDNN repo (a baseline itself) but no dedicated repo was opened, so repo_url is null and license is unconfirmed. Compiler flags not stated; FP32 matmul is slower than primitives.
name: oneDNN Graph Compiler
baseline: oneDNN primitives with post-op fusion; TVM auto-scheduler
workload: Tensor compiler fusing MLP and MHA subgraphs, BERT-Large and DLRM end to end.
claimed_speedup: BERT Large 1.12x and DLRM 1.15x over oneDNN post-op fusion; 2.4x (MLP) and 6.2x (MHA) over TVM; FP32 matmul 4% worse than primitives, Int8 6% better
found_via: WebSearch: arXiv attention kernel CPU C++ library outperforms oneDNN Eigen

tradeoffs: Expression-template design; limited feature set versus Stan Math.
caveats: Benchmark repo lists versions (Adept 2.0.8, Stan Math 3.3.0, FastAD 3) but CPU model and flags missing; numbers in the speedup field come from the arXiv abstract (2102.03681), not the benchmark page. Baselines are not the listed ML incumbents.
name: FastAD
workload: Expression-template forward/reverse-mode automatic differentiation versus other C++ AD libraries on nine tests (sum, product, log-sum-exp, matrix ops, normal log-pdf, regression, stochastic volatility).
claimed_speedup: 2-10 times faster than Adept and 2-19 times faster than Stan; README claims orders of magnitude over Adept, Stan Math, ADOL-C, CppAD, Sacado
found_via: WebSearch: arXiv automatic differentiation C++ library benchmark faster than Eigen autodiff Stan math CppAD Enzyme

hardware: AWS c4.8xlarge, hyperthreading and Turbo Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Compiler plugin on statically analyzable LLVM/MLIR; works across C/C++/Rust/Julia/Fortran.
caveats: NeurIPS 2020 paper; compiler flags not read. License type not shown on the page I opened (LICENSE file exists); verify before copying. Baselines are AD tools not ML kernels. Advantage attributed largely to optimizing before AD.
name: Enzyme
baseline: Adept and Tapenade (and AD on unoptimized IR)
workload: LLVM-level reverse-mode AD on ADBench (BA, LSTM, GMM) and integrator/FFT/Brusselator tests.
claimed_speedup: geometric mean 4.5x speedup over AD on IR before optimization; outperforms Tapenade and Adept across tested benchmarks (no per-test ratio read)
found_via: WebSearch: Enzyme automatic differentiation LLVM C++ paper speedup vs Adept CppAD
